_readme: Technical Product Marketing, Version 1.3: the rebuilt case study through 01 Hero, 02 Foundation, 03 the transitional statement, 04 Website, 05 Technical documentation, 06 the flagship animation campaign, 07 Selected Writing and 08 the conclusion, then Contact. Copy is John's approved wording from the V1 concept, the V1.1, V1.2 and V1.3 briefs and the V1.2 delta brief (October 12 and 13, 2026); `accent` names the one phrase of a headline set in the accent color and `em` the one phrase of a paragraph set a little heavier (V1.3: a handful of each across the page, never both on one phrase); the chapter notes under the documentation walkthrough are drafted from the brief's confirmed facts and are open to John's edits. The foundation library lists twelve named documents in the brief's order, with display numbers 00 to 11 (not their Linear numbers); no document body is read, quoted or published.

hero._hero: Headline, paragraph and the seven scope terms on the left, the abstract narrative-system object on the right (V1.3); no kicker and no media. The headline never changes.
hero.headline: Building the system behind the message.
hero.copy: I built the strategic foundation that turned Bolt Liquidity’s technical complexity into a clear market narrative, then carried it across documentation, web experiences, articles, and campaigns.

foundation._headline: Always two lines, broken where the brief breaks it.
headline: Before the message
comes the foundation.
foundation.copy: Before a product can be explained externally, it needs a shared internal language. For Bolt Liquidity, I built that language from stakeholder interviews and product research, shaping the positioning, claims, proof points, and narrative architecture behind every public-facing expression.
foundation._documents: In the brief's order, from internal input through market understanding, strategic definition, governance and expression. Each document has its own muted accent (its strip and its faded icon) and its own icon; no two neighbors share a hue family. The interview count is not published.
foundation._depth: Unlabeled, neutral covers after the last named document: no number, title, subline or icon, only the suggestion that the library runs deeper.

statement.copy: Once the product language is clear, it guides every expression that follows: the website, technical documentation, articles, campaigns, and content that bring the product to market.
statement._highlight: The page's one animated highlight (V1.3): once the statement has been revealed, a translucent teal sweeps behind this clause, the one that says how the shared language guides every public-facing expression.

writing.title: Selected Writing

articles.title: The Missing Price Layer
articles._source: https://x.com/BoltLiquidity/status/2085335475137417401 (August 6, 2026). Excerpt from the section Fragmentation is not the disease, taken from the Google Doc the article was published from (The Missing Price Layer, last edited 47 minutes before the post).
excerpt: Traditional finance is fragmented too. US equities trade across dozens of exchanges and alternative trading venues; the same stock is quoted in many places at once by different firms, and nobody treats this as a crisis. Fragmentation never went away there either.

The venues kept competing. Market makers kept quoting independently. But every participant ended up operating inside the same price discovery system, which meant competition stayed fragmented while price formation became coordinated. Crypto has the first half of that and not the second.

articles.title: DeFi’s Billion-Dollar Problem
articles._source: https://x.com/BoltLiquidity/status/1968407791170687124 (September 17, 2025). Excerpt from the section What Causes Slippage?, taken from the Google Doc the article was written in (Twitter Ad Article, last edited September 4, 2025).
excerpt: In most DeFi protocols, prices are determined by automated market makers (AMMs), where the asset ratios and liquidity depth in pools dictate the price. While AMMs were a breakthrough in DeFi, enabling permissionless trading without relying on order books, these pools only work efficiently when they’re deep. And because bootstrapping deep liquidity is expensive, it’s rarely available outside the most heavily traded pairs.

When liquidity is shallow, trades cause larger price movements, known as slippage. The bigger the trade, the worse the slippage becomes. As a result, users often receive fewer tokens than expected, a quiet loss hidden in the execution.

conclusion._conclusion: 08 The closing frame (V1.3): a synthesis, not a summary. Only the way on to the next case study follows the copy; no metrics, services, credits or roles.
conclusion.headline: One foundation. Every expression aligned.
conclusion.copy: The work began with a shared product language and carried through the website, technical documentation, and flagship campaign, giving every public-facing expression the same strategic foundation.
